paragraphs: R. Ezra (bar—so Yalkut, Shemot§166), son of R. Avtolos [with the preceding bar: grandson, as in the printed Bavli], tenth in descent from R. Elazar ben Azaryah, himself tenth from Ezra. Rashi: R. Elazar ben Azaryah was tenth from Ezra the scribe. He came before R. Perida (see his entry); he [Ezra] was a Torah scholar and expounded: 'Let the mighty one come and exact payment for the mighty, from the mighty, through the mighty,' Menaḥot 53a. Yuḥasin [under R. Elazar ben Azaryah in Seder HaDorot, and tannaim under alef] notes a reading R. Azaryah ben Avtolos, father of R. Elazar ben Azaryah, as the visitor; likewise Responsa Rivash §94 [Azaryah, but Avtolos’s grandson and Elazar’s tenth descendant]. To exclude that reading, it says R. Azaryah was tenth from R. Elazar, who was tenth from Ezra, since R. Perida lived in R. Ammi's time, and Tefillat HaShaḥar explicitly calls R. Elazar tenth from Ezra. Some confusion appears there, but this is Yuḥasin's principal intention. The argument that R. Azaryah—our text, R. Ezra—could not be R. Elazar's father because he visited R. Perida in R. Ammi's time can be answered on Maimonides' view that R. Perida was born before the destruction (see his entry). Yuḥasin suggests Maimonides read that R. Elazar's father R. Azaryah visited him. Do not wonder at R. Perida living in R. Ammi's time: he lived more than four hundred years. Confused readings generated this argument: R. Ezra was written R. Azaryah, a reading preserved in parentheses in Ein Yaakov, alongside bracketed Ezra. Our Gemara, R. Ezra ben Avtolos, leaves no room to mistake him for R. Elazar ben Azaryah's father.
